stories.summary: In the early 1980s (his father died in 1984), Ajay was at home when an American from Corning Glass came to meet his father. Corning wanted to set up a factory in India to make glass, expecting demand for things like television picture tubes. His father told him it wouldn't happen, because the Indian state banned this and banned that. The visitor was baffled that a government would want to stop a company from building factories in its country.
stories.insight: Ajay's first encounter with FDI was watching it get refused. A foreign businessman found India's hostility to his investment simply incomprehensible. Amit reframes the episode's subject on the spot: what Ajay really loves is not FDI but freedom.
stories.quote: And this guy was very baffled, why would the government want to prevent us from building factories in India.

stories.topic: Nokia Packs Up and Leaves Tamil Nadu
stories.summary: Nokia built a manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu, exactly the kind of foreign factory India says it wants. The Indian state then went after the company with income-tax demands and asset freezes, and eventually Nokia packed up and left.
stories.insight: Welcoming foreign investors is not enough. If the state does not wall foreign firms off from the treatment it normally inflicts on Indian companies, even a marquee investment walks out. Ajay sees this as a failure of intellectual clarity about why FDI works in the first place.
stories.quote: the Indian state went after them with income tax and freezing of assets and so on. And in the end, Nokia packed up and left.

stories.topic: How Bangladesh Learned the Garment Business
stories.summary: Taiwanese and South Korean companies were the first to set up garment operations in Bangladesh. Local people who worked there learned the business, then stepped out and started garment firms of their own, and the industry spread from there.
stories.insight: The real prize of FDI is not the foreign factory but the knowledge it leaves behind. That knowledge sits with workers, not with the foreign firm, and it spreads as they switch jobs and start companies.
stories.quote: in Bangladesh, there were first Taiwanese and South Korean companies who started garment activities. And then the people who learned those garment businesses stepped out and started their own businesses

stories.topic: From George Fernandes to Xi Jinping: The Same Mistake Twice
stories.summary: Ajay recalls that George Fernandes drove IBM (which supported the IBM mainframes used in India) and Coca-Cola out of India by imposing conditions: forced technology transfer, a forced IPO in India, a forced joint venture. Decades later, he says, the same kinds of rules crept back into Xi Jinping's China, undoing Deng Xiaoping's promise to leave foreign firms alone. FDI into China collapsed.
stories.insight: Countries keep relearning that FDI dies when the state can't resist meddling. China's FDI miracle was not a permanent feature of China. It rested on a political commitment, and it ended when that commitment did.
stories.quote: All these kinds of things started creeping back in the world of Xi Jinping. So this is the loss of clarity.

recommendations.item: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Episode 104 of Everything is Everything)

recommendations.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah

recommendations.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's co-authored paper on how the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model reverses in Indian software.
recommendations.reason: It shows that in Indian software, firms doing outbound FDI (body shoppers) are less productive than pure exporters. The standard internationalisation ladder is turned upside down.

core_ideas.explanation: FDI means a foreigner holding a substantial, long-term stake in an Indian production arrangement. The OECD and IMF line is 10% equity: 9% is portfolio investment, 10% is FDI. Several things also count: a foreign parent's loan to its Indian subsidiary, a foreign private equity fund's 11% stake in a fully Indian company, and profits that a foreign-owned Indian operation reinvests instead of repatriating (booked as fresh FDI that year). 'FDI in India' and 'FDI by India' are separate flows.
core_ideas.quote: There is a definition which has been agreed to by the OECD and the IMF that the minimum equity shareholding should be 10%.

core_ideas.concept: The Seven FDI Numbers and the Propagandist's Menu
core_ideas.explanation: The balance of payments produces seven FDI numbers: gross inflow, repatriation and net for FDI in India; gross outflow, money coming back and net for FDI by India; and 'net net' overall. Propagandists of every stripe cherry-pick whichever one flatters their story. Ajay's tell for propaganda is a chart or table labelled simply 'FDI' without saying which series it is.
core_ideas.quote: If you say FDI, you're a propagandist. Okay, you have to be precise.

core_ideas.concept: The Dream of FDI: An Honest Enclave
core_ideas.explanation: FDI's magic comes from a country admitting its institutions are bad and building an escape valve. It sets aside, say, one square kilometre where there is no local labour law, no tax harassment, no visa trouble and no customs duties on goods in or out. A bonded warehouse is the cleanest version of this. In return, the state collects only income tax on workers' wages and GST on their spending, and the workers get jobs. Deng Xiaoping's insight was that fixing China's company law and taxes would take a century, so China built a trusted, predictable interface for foreigners in the meantime. Ajay says India never said these paragraphs to itself clearly.
core_ideas.quote: So it's not true that Chinese FDI operates in bad institutions. FDI into China operates under good institutions because the Chinese state is able to back off.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge Diffusion Is FDI's Ultimate Prize
core_ideas.explanation: If knowledge is what drives a society forward, foreign firms are where much of it gets made. Workers learn the global productivity frontier and how globalised production works. That knowledge stays with them rather than with the company, and it spreads when they move to other jobs or start firms.
core_ideas.quote: Then we should view FDI as the crucible where the knowledge is made.

core_ideas.concept: It's Unfair to Indian Firms, and That's the Point
core_ideas.explanation: Treating foreign firms exactly like Indian ones, with the same regulators, capital controls and visa problems, removes the point of FDI. The bargain only works if foreigners get better treatment than domestic businesses. Amit adds that this is no argument against fixing India's institutions, a fight that continues. Meanwhile, 'little islands of freedom' are worth having, and the perfect shouldn't be the enemy of the good.
core_ideas.quote: The magic of FDI is not in having foreign companies. stand in line and be treated by Indian regulators and Indian capital controls and Indian passport visa problems, just like anybody else. Then what's the point?

core_ideas.concept: 'Hot Money' Fear Is Insecurity, Not Analysis
core_ideas.explanation: Indian policy circles call FDI the good guy and portfolio investment dangerous 'hot money'. Ajay rejects this on three counts. Foreigners already know India's weaknesses, and those are priced in as lower security prices. Foreign investors are not a monolithic bloc: every day sees large gross buying and selling with a tiny net, all absorbed by the market. And India has never had a big crisis from foreign portfolio exit; in shocks like the COVID lockdown, Indians and foreigners sold alike.
core_ideas.quote: The fact that a portfolio investor can sell securities and leave frightens an insecure Indian.

core_ideas.concept: Portfolio Investment Needs Better Institutions Than FDI
core_ideas.explanation: FDI can work with a short rulebook and a state that backs off. Portfolio investment has no way around local institutions. It needs trustworthy accounting, audit, a stock market and a depository, so an investor in Tokyo can trust that a piece of paper really means they own shares. That is why China never got portfolio investment going while India, with about 150 years of accounting tradition, can. Ajay also treats FDI and FPI as different technologies: governments should build institutions, not decree which flows are good.
core_ideas.quote: So contrary to the feelings of many an Indian economist, it is FDI that demands a lower institutional quality and FPI. demands a higher institutional quality.

core_ideas.concept: Who in India Wants Which Foreign Money
core_ideas.explanation: India's elite reacts differently to the two kinds of foreign money. FDI means competition: a foreign carmaker hurts Premier Padmini, and Indian retail resents Amazon and Walmart. Portfolio investment means more buyers for Indian firms' shares and bonds, and a lower cost of capital. So the incumbent business community welcomes FPI and resists FDI. The insight is credited to Ila Patnaik. Ajay thinks a pure export enclave would be politically harmless and has failed only for lack of intellectual clarity.
core_ideas.quote: So for the Indian rich, FDI is not interesting. FDI is not attractive because it is competition for their own businesses.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Jagdish Bhagwati's term, which he raised in the early 1990s when the first FDI surge reached India. Erect trade barriers and foreigners will set up minimal plants inside them, assembling semi-knocked-down cars and selling into the protected market. It looks like FDI but is really arbitrage around policy, and much of India's auto industry fits this pattern. Trade liberalisation comes first: either run a duty-free enclave, or allow mainline FDI with no trade barriers.
core_ideas.quote: Actually, they're just arbitraging around the tariff and non-tariff barriers in India.

core_ideas.concept: Bilateral Investment Treaties as Insurance and a Self-Slap
core_ideas.explanation: Foreigners don't trust a state that did Vodafone-style retrospective taxation. Bilateral investment treaties bridge that gap: India promises to compensate foreign investors when any level of the Indian state expropriates them. Paying out $1 billion a year to stabilise $100 billion of FDI is a cheap insurance premium, and the slap disciplines the state. But officials took lost cases personally, a 'sovereign right to expropriate' machismo set in, and the 2016 model BIT abandoned many good ideas. India is now increasingly hostile to such treaties.
core_ideas.quote: I also will observe in passing that it's actually brilliantly incentive compatible for the Indian state to pay money when the Indian state misbehaves.

core_ideas.concept: The Anti-Foreigner Streak and the Cult of Third-Worldism
core_ideas.explanation: India's distrust of foreign capital comes from a deep anti-Western streak and a third-worldism that casts multinationals as exploiters of helpless workers. A newer arrogance adds that India is so important foreigners must come anyway. Ajay argues that success lies in embracing the global frontier. Amit adds that all trade and human connection is positive-sum.
core_ideas.quote: There is a deep anti-foreigner streak in India. There is a deep anti-Western streak in India. And in deep ways this has fed into Indian failure

core_ideas.concept: The HMY Ladder and Its Indian Software Inversion
core_ideas.explanation: The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model ranks firms by productivity: the weakest stay domestic, better ones export, the best do FDI abroad. That gives a simple test of an Indian firm: domestic, exporter, or multinational? Hundreds of Indian firms are now multinationals. Indian software reverses the ladder. Firms that sit in India while foreign business comes to them are the most productive. Those that do outbound FDI by 'body shopping' staff into the UK and Germany are weaker.
core_ideas.quote: It's upside down that FDI Indian software companies are worse than exporting Indian software companies.

core_ideas.explanation: The breakdown of the China model and America's tariff turmoil have reshaped the world economy, and Ajay sees a rare opening for India. A surge in FDI or goods exports does not yet show up in the data, but he believes the conditions for change are now in place.
core_ideas.quote: I think twenty twenty five is an important moment in India's history.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens by insisting 'this episode is not about money, this episode is about love'. Ajay has confided five great loves: firm productivity, capital account openness, inflation targeting and, above all, FDI. When Ajay says 'inflation targeting', Amit cracks, 'Oh my God, you almost came as you said that.' He then asks, mock-romantically, 'Tell me about the first time you guys met. You and FDI.'
Ajay on the Chinese model: 'Deng Xiaoping's dream was there will be no Xi Jinping. We will fix China one day.'

After Ajay declares anyone who labels a chart just 'FDI' a propagandist, Amit says: 'You have terrified me. I'm never gonna say FDI in front of you again. Straight away it will be like net inflow, gross inflow.'
Ajay explains market churn with a foreign seller matched by 'a Bengali who is buying'. Amit quips: 'Some foreign portfolio investors are Bengali. We are everywhere.'

Ajay applies a love maxim to capital flows: 'If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn't, it never was. That is the right approach to apply to all the great loves of your life, whether FDI or FPI.' He later mocks the anti-FPI economists as asking, 'will you love me next week?'
Amit sums up the FDI-versus-FPI debate: 'On one side of the debate you have securities. On the other side you have insecurities.'

Amit recalls his first reaction to SEZs: 'my purest libertarian mind reacted by saying, Why do we need SEZ? A whole country should be an SEZ. Into that heaven of freedom, my father, let my country awake.' He caps it with a famous line of verse.

Amit asks why there can't be world-class Indian firms 'when There are world class Indian YouTube shows'. Ajay declares the show 'an exporting show' with a 30% overseas audience: 'You have graduated.' Amit panics that this will invite an income-tax raid: 'My head is spinning, bro.'
Amit, closing the love metaphor: 'the good thing is that FDI is liberal with her affections. We do not have to compete. We can both get FDI.'
Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (dir. Aziz Mirza) gives the chapter its title and metaphor: 'Raju Wants to be gentlemen. Indian firms want to be global firms.'
The Vodafone retrospective taxation episode, which Amit cites as the kind of 'nonsense' that destroys the predictability foreign investors need.
Premier Padmini stands in for the protected Indian incumbent threatened by a foreigner making cars in India. Indian retail's anger at Amazon and Walmart is the modern version.
Cafe Coffee Day in Vienna, Ajay's example of 'FDI by India'. He says he has a photograph to prove it.
